This post covers the core syntax every Python program uses: variables, primitive types, operators, conditionals, and loops. Python's defining visual feature — meaningful indentation — is introduced and explained. By the end, you can write any control-flow logic you'd expect from a beginner book.
Series map: 00 Setup → 01 Syntax (this post) → 02 Data Structures → 03 Functions & Modules → 04 OOP → 05 Files & Exceptions → (future).

Declare variables and understand dynamic typing.
Use the six core primitive types: int, float, bool, str, None, bytes.
Use arithmetic, comparison, logical, and assignment operators.
Write if/elif/else, for, and while blocks.
Understand indentation as syntax (not decoration).
Use break, continue, and else on loops.

Variable — a name bound to a value.
Dynamic typing — variable types are checked at runtime, not declaration time.
Type hint — optional annotation (x: int = 5) — ignored at runtime, used by tools.
Mutable / immutable — whether a value can be changed in place.

x = 5 # int
pi = 3.14159 # float
name = "Ada" # str
is_ready = True # bool
nothing = None # NoneType
No type declaration required. You can rebind to a different type:
x = 5
x = "now a string" # legal in Python

x: int = 5
name: str = "Ada"
These are hints — Python ignores them at runtime. Tools like mypy, pyright, and your IDE use them for static analysis. Use them in real code; skip them in throwaway scripts.
Trick: if you print(type(x)), Python tells you the runtime type. Great for debugging "wait, why is this a string?" surprises.

Type · Example · Note
int · 42, -7, 0, 10_000 · Arbitrary precision — no overflow! 2**100 works fine.
float · 3.14, 1e-5, 2.0 · IEEE 754 double.
bool · True, False · A subclass of int: True == 1, False == 0.
str · "hello", 'world', """multi-line""" · Immutable, Unicode by default.
None · None · The "no value" singleton.
bytes · b"raw", b"\x00\xff" · Immutable sequence of 8-bit values.

s = "Hello"
len(s) # 5
s.upper() # "HELLO"
s[0] # "H"
s[-1] # "o" (negative = from end)
s[1:4] # "ell" (slice)
"He" in s # True
s + " World" # "Hello World"
s * 3 # "HelloHelloHello"

name = "Ada"
age = 30
f"{name} is {age}" # "Ada is 30"
f"{age * 2}" # "60"
f"{3.14159:.2f}" # "3.14" (2 decimal places)
f"{42:>5}" # " 42" (right-align width 5)
f"{name=}" # "name='Ada'" (debug form, Python 3.8+)
Trick: the {var=} debug form is the single most-used Python 3.8+ feature. f"{user_id=} {total=}" gives "user_id=42 total=99.50" — perfect for logging.

Op · Meaning · Example
+ · add · 3 + 4 → 7
- · subtract · 7 - 2 → 5
* · multiply · 3 * 4 → 12
/ · true divide · 7 / 2 → 3.5
// · floor divide · 7 // 2 → 3
% · modulo · 7 % 3 → 1
** · power · 2 ** 10 → 1024

==, !=, <, >, <=, >= — return bool. Python supports chained comparison:
if 0 < x < 10: # legal, means 0 < x AND x < 10
...

and, or, not. They short-circuit:
x and y # if x is falsy, returns x; else returns y
x or y # if x is truthy, returns x; else returns y
not x # True if x is falsy
Falsy values: False, 0, 0.0, "", [], {}, (), None. Everything else is truthy.

a = [1, 2, 3]
b = [1, 2, 3]
a == b # True (same content)
a is b # False (different objects)
a is None # idiomatic way to check for None — use `is`, not `==`

This is the rule that shocks beginners coming from C-family languages. Python uses indentation (not {} or begin/end) to define blocks.
if x > 0:
print("positive") # this line is inside the if
print("still inside") # this too
print("outside the if") # this is after
Rules:
All lines in the same block must have exactly the same indentation.
Standard is 4 spaces per level (PEP 8).
Never mix tabs and spaces. Most editors auto-convert.
A colon : introduces a new block (after if, for, while, def, class, try, etc.).
Where I got stuck: I once spent 30 minutes debugging a script that "just didn't run the loop". The culprit: a tab character on one line where the rest used spaces. Python silently disagrees about whether they're equal. Modern editors highlight whitespace; turn it on.

status = "adult" if age >= 18 else "minor"
Read it left-to-right: "value, if condition, else alternative".

match command:
case "start":
print("starting")
case "stop" | "halt":
print("stopping")
case _:
print("unknown")
The _ is a catch-all. match also supports pattern destructuring — covered in a future advanced post.

Python's for always iterates over an iterable (sequence, generator, etc.). It is not the C-style for(i=0; i<10; i++).
for fruit in ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]:
print(fruit)
for i in range(5): # 0, 1, 2, 3, 4
print(i)
for i in range(2, 8): # 2..7
print(i)
for i in range(0, 20, 3): # 0, 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 (step=3)
print(i)

for i, name in enumerate(["Ada", "Bob", "Cy"]):
print(i, name)
# 0 Ada
# 1 Bob
# 2 Cy

names = ["Ada", "Bob"]
ages = [30, 25]
for name, age in zip(names, ages):
print(name, age)

# single-line comment
"""
This is a triple-quoted string. When it's the first thing in a function,
class, or module, it becomes the *docstring* — accessible via help() or __doc__.
"""
def add(a, b):
"""Return the sum of a and b."""
return a + b
help(add) # shows the docstring

Given a positive integer (input from user), print the sum of its digits. Example: 123 → 6.
Solution
n = int(input("Number: "))
total = 0
while n > 0:
total += n % 10
n //= 10
print(total)

The computer picks a random number 1–100. The user guesses; you print "too high", "too low", or "correct!". Limit to 7 guesses.
Solution
import random
target = random.randint(1, 100)
for attempt in range(1, 8):
g = int(input(f"Guess {attempt}/7: "))
if g == target:
print(f"Correct in {attempt} guesses!")
break
print("too low" if g < target else "too high")
else:
print(f"Out of guesses. It was {target}.")

Falsy values · False, 0, "", [], {}, None
